prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 2.1-5 Schematic of Colored Paving for Bus-Only Lanes 2.1.6 Bus Stops Bus bay stops may be divided into direct stops and bay stops. 1. Direct Bus Stop The lane width of a direct bus stop shall generally not be less than 3.00 m, and shall not be less than 2.75 m where conditions are constrained. Figure 2.1-6 Schematic of a Direct Bus Stop 2. Bay Bus Stop Where space within the road is insufficient, the road red line may be locally widened. Where the red line is constrained, a bay bus stop may be provided by reducing lane width and through integrated design with roadside space. Figure 2.1-7 Schematic of a Single Bay Bus Stop In addition to single bay stops, there are also double bay bus stops. Generally, a double bay bus stop consists of a main stop and an auxiliary stop. The main stop is a bay stop, while the auxiliary stop is a direct stop where vehicles stop directly. 30 Figure 2.1-8 Schematic of a Double Bay Bus Stop 2.1.7 Roadside Parking Lane The general rules for parking space arrangement are as follows: 1. At unsignalized intersections where the approach or departure road is a single lane, no parking spaces shall be set within 10 m of the straight curb segment on the intersection approach side; no parking spaces shall be set within 8 m of the straight curb segment on the departure side. 2. At channelized intersections, no parking spaces shall be set within the channelized area and within 5 m outside it. 3. No parking spaces shall be set within 6 m on the departure side and 10 m on the approach side, measured from the starting point of the straight curb segment on both sides of a parcel entrance/exit. 4. No parking spaces shall be set within 8 m upstream and 6 m downstream of the vehicle stop line in the direction of approach to a pedestrian crossing. 5. No parking spaces shall be set within 25 m before and 15 m after a bus stop platform. 6. No parking spaces shall be set in the ground space corresponding to a radius of 1.5 m from the center of the manhole cover of underground utility access shafts. 7. The distance between parking spaces before and after a fire hydrant shall not be less than 30 m, and the distance from the nearest parking space to the fire hydrant shall not be less than 2.5 m. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Landscape-recreation roads Definition: roads with prominent landscape features, along which parks, green spaces, and recreational facilities are distributed. Design focus: create road scenes with smooth slow-mobility circulation, beautiful scenery, openness and transparency, and convenient facilities. Historic-style streets and lanes Definition: streets and lanes that preserve abundant cultural relics, concentrate historic buildings, can more completely reflect the traditional spatial pattern, and have a certain scale. Design focus: prioritize slow mobility, continue the historic and cultural character, and enhance vitality and activity. Smart-city demonstration roads Definition: roads that, through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, achieve deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, and serve as a showcase and promotion of Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. Design focus: based on an integrated framework of the traffic-participant subsystem, roadside subsystem, and central subsystem. Emphasis is placed on “the road” and “the cloud,” providing intelligent services for “vehicles” and “people.” Comprehensive roads Definition: roads with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and with characteristics of two or more road types. Design focus: carry out targeted road design according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. 7 Road-type functional traffic corridors Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • The design should respond to the needs of different traffic modes, including motor vehicles, non-motorized traffic, public transport, freight transport, and pedestrian traffic, with a coordinated allocation of space. • At intersections where signal lights are installed, allow motor vehicles to pass with longer distances and higher speeds as much as possible, reducing crossings by motor vehicles and pedestrians. Spatial requirements: • Intersections should be organized in a clear and orderly manner; curb extensions may be set up, pedestrian crossing distances shortened, and pedestrian visibility improved. • The roadside interface should mainly be non-open, and road greenery, screens, separation, and transparent visual-control effects may be used. Direct Bus Stop The lane width of a direct bus stop shall generally not be less than 3.00 m, and shall not be less than 2.75 m where conditions are constrained. Figure 2.1-6 Schematic of a Direct Bus Stop 2. Bay Bus Stop Where space within the road is insufficient, the road red line may be locally widened. Where the red line is constrained, a bay bus stop may be provided by reducing lane width and through integrated design with roadside space. Figure 2.1-7 Schematic of a Single Bay Bus Stop In addition to single bay stops, there are also double bay bus stops. Generally, a double bay bus stop consists of a main stop and an auxiliary stop. The main stop is a bay stop, while the auxiliary stop is a direct stop where vehicles stop directly. 30 Figure 2.1-8 Schematic of a Double Bay Bus Stop 2.1.7 Roadside Parking Lane The general rules for parking space arrangement are as follows: 1. At unsignalized intersections where the approach or departure road is a single lane, no parking spaces shall be set within 10 m of the straight curb segment on the intersection approach side; no parking spaces shall be set within 8 m of the straight curb segment on the departure side. 2. At channelized intersections, no parking spaces shall be set within the channelized area and within 5 m outside it. 3. No parking spaces shall be set within 6 m on the departure side and 10 m on the approach side, measured from the starting point of the straight curb segment on both sides of a parcel entrance/exit. 4. No parking spaces shall be set within 8 m upstream and 6 m downstream of the vehicle stop line in the direction of approach to a pedestrian crossing. 5. No parking spaces shall be set within 25 m before and 15 m after a bus stop platform. 6. No parking spaces shall be set in the ground space corresponding to a radius of 1.5 m from the center of the manhole cover of underground utility access shafts. 7. The distance between parking spaces before and after a fire hydrant shall not be less than 30 m, and the distance from the nearest parking space to the fire hydrant shall not be less than 2.5 m.
